abstract: Dietary ethanol has long been proposed as a selective force shaping the diets and physiology of tropical frugivores and nectarivores, yet this idea has rested on measurements from only a few species and sites. Here, we present the first global survey of ethanol in wild fruits and flowers (591 and 37 species, respectively, across 18 countries) and test ecological and phylogenetic predictors of its variation. We detected ethanol in the ripened fruits of 72% of angiosperm species (211 species, N [≥] 3 per species; 0.021% - 3.9% alcohol by volume (ABV)). Ethanol was also detected in the flowers of 12 species (0.037% - 0.73% ABV). Maximum fruit ethanol varied with temperature, humidity, and phylogenetic relatedness, and it was higher in ripe fruits collected from the forest floor relative to their canopy counterparts. We then extrapolated potential daily ethanol consumption for 10 primate species. Estimated maximum daily ethanol ingestion for primates ranged from negligible to 0.72 g/kg/day on average (equivalent to 5.1 international standard drinks, 10 g ethanol each, for a 70 kg human). Our findings show that ethanol is widespread in plant reproductive tissues and shaped by both phylogeny and environment, supporting the hypothesis that dietary ethanol has been a pervasive selective pressure on fruit- and nectar-feeding animals.
hook: Ethanol turns up in 72% of wild fruit species sampled worldwide, at up to 3.9% alcohol by volume.

summary: A survey of 591 fruit species and 37 flower species in 18 countries found ethanol in most ripe fruit, more on the forest floor and in warm, humid places. Extrapolating, some primates could take in the equivalent of about five drinks a day for a human. Those intake figures are estimates, not measured consumption.
title: Pervasive ethanol in the fruits and floral nectars consumed by tropical frugivores
